content: Nursemaid's elbow is a condition where the radius, one of the bones in the forearm, becomes dislocated at the elbow joint. This type of dislocation occurs when the bone slips out of its normal position within the joint. It is also referred to as a radial head dislocation. When a child experiences nursemaid's elbow, they typically begin crying immediately due to pain in the elbow and will refuse to use the affected arm. The child may hold the arm in a slightly bent position at the elbow, keeping it close to their abdomen. While the child may still move their shoulder, they will avoid moving the elbow. In some cases, the initial pain may subside, and the child may stop crying, but they will continue to avoid using the elbow. This condition is most commonly seen in children under the age of five. It often occurs when a child is pulled or lifted too forcefully by the hand or wrist. For example, this can happen when lifting a child over a curb or step by one arm. Other potential causes include breaking a fall with the arm, rolling over in an unusual manner, or swinging a child by the arms during play. Once the elbow has dislocated, it is more likely to happen again, particularly within the first three to four weeks following the initial injury. However, nursemaid's elbow is rare after the age of five, as the joints and surrounding structures become stronger, and children are less likely to be in situations that could lead to this injury. In rare cases, older children or adults may experience this condition, typically as a result of a forearm fracture. Children under the age of five are at the highest risk for nursemaid's elbow. A healthcare provider can diagnose the condition by examining the child. A key sign is the inability to rotate the arm at the elbow so that the palm faces upward, as well as difficulty fully bending the elbow. If you suspect that your child has a dislocated elbow or if they refuse to use one arm, it is important to seek medical attention promptly. In some cases, the elbow may return to its normal position on its own, but it is still essential to have the child evaluated by a healthcare provider. Do not attempt to straighten or reposition the arm yourself, as this could cause further harm. Applying an ice pack to the elbow and immobilizing the area, including the shoulder and wrist, can help minimize discomfort while waiting for medical care. The child should be taken to a doctor’s office or emergency room, where a healthcare provider will gently manipulate the elbow to restore its normal position. This involves flexing the elbow and rotating the forearm so that the palm faces upward. If the condition recurs frequently, the healthcare provider may teach parents how to safely correct the dislocation at home. If nursemaid's elbow is left untreated, the child may experience permanent limitations in elbow movement. However, with proper treatment, there is typically no long-term damage. In rare cases, complications may arise that restrict arm movement. To prevent nursemaid's elbow, avoid lifting a child by one arm, whether by the wrist or hand. Instead, lift the child from under the arms, by the upper arms, or using both arms. Do not swing children by their hands or forearms.
